docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This is subsystem A1 of the duck. The subsystem constitutes the OLED screen and buttons used to communicate direction and controll of multiple subsystems in the boat we have created.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• This subsystem will be connected to A2, a wireless subsystem, that connecte to the whole daisy chain in the boat. Both "A" subsystems are the whole controller that we use. This will be outside the boat and connected to a wall jack for power. We anticipated that this would be on a bigger boat, like a cruise ship, and the smaller boat would go out and survey the outer hull of the boat and the surrounding area.
  • For morte information about other subsystems and the whole team project here is the team report..

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This block diagram is for the display and control ESP32 for the rover. This subsystem will use serial cvode to send information to the rover that the rover will then articulate to move and travel or do specific actions. Since this piece is not connected to the roiver, it will need a seperate power system with voltage regulators. THis will also need the OLED screen that will display serial information to the user.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: There are 9 pins, 1 OLED, and two LEDs that make the main part of the block diagram. 3 pins are for boot, enable, and debugging. These are the basics of a schematic with an esp32. The LEDs are also for debugging and communication throughout the systems. The 6 other pins are split between direction (4 pins) and spares. The spares are for if other pins do not work.

docs.title: Decicions for the Changes
docs.text: Everything was still the same after making the PCB/ The block diagram had the components it needed and there was no change in the main part. The change comes in with the buttons. The spare buttons were used, not because of other buttons being broken, because we needed more prompts from the A1 subsystem for movements of other subsystems. This came to place because the team kept growing even after this assignment.

docs.title: ESP32
docs.text: This is the brain of the subsystem. It will take information from the other subsystems and display it onto the OLED screen. The ESP32 will also use the buttons to send signals and information to the other subsystems to tell them to move.

docs.title: OLED Screen
docs.text: This screen will display serial information from other subsystems. It will also display what motiuon buttons are being pressed to show that it is trying to send commands to the rover.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: Other than the main debug, boot, and enable pins, there are 6 other buttons. 4 of these buttons are forward, bafckward, left, and right. The other 2 are spare buttons if they are needed or a button breaks.

docs.title: LEDs
docs.text: One LED is for debugging. The other is a LED that pairs with the other subsystems and their LED. This shows that the system is taking and recieving information.

docs.title: Connections
docs.text: The 8 pin connectors attach to the other subsystem of the controller. This enables both subsystems to give and recieve serial communication.

docs.title: Module Messages
docs.text: The following sections document the messages sent and received from A1 subsystem.

docs.title: My Role
docs.text:
My role is to send directional movement to each subsystem for them to receive and use that information. I will then receive the rest of the subsystem's messeges.

Here are all the messeges and message types:

message type byte 1 (uint8_t) description 1 Set steering angle in degrees - Sent from A1 to B2 as a response to user input. Upon recieving, B2 will move the rudders to the indicated position. 2 Set steering throttle percentage - Sent from A1 to B1 as a response to user input. Upon recieving, B1 will adjust the speed of the propellers to the desired percentage. 3 Set camera angle in degrees - Sent from A1 to C2 as a response to user input. Upon recieving, C2 will move the camera gimbal to the indicated position. 4 Take picture. Sent from A1 to C1 as a response to user input. Upon recieving, C1 will take a picture and save it to an SD card. 5 Send speed data in m/s - Sent periodically from C3 to A1. Upon recieving, A1 will update the display. 6 Send distance data in cm - Sent periodically from D2 to A1. Upon recieving, A1 will update the display. 7 Send temperature data in celsius - Sent periodically from D1 to A1. Upon recieving, A1 will update the display. 8 Send camera angle data data in degrees - Sent periodically from C3 to C2. Used for gimbal stabilization. 9 Bluetooth communication error - Sent from both A2 and A3 as a broadcast as a result of failing 3 bluetooth heartbeat checks. Upon recieving, B2 sets angle to 0, B1 sets throttle to 0, and A1 shows an error on screen. 10 Bluetooth relay data - Sent between A2 and A3 (bidirectional). Contains a relayed message and relayed sender/reciever IDs. 11 Bluetooth heartbeat - Sent periodically from A2 to A3. Upon recieving, A3 will send this message back. If neither board recieves a heartbeat within a set interval, heartbeat failure will be recorded. 12 Rollcall - Debugging broadcast message triggered by pushing the 'debug' button on any subsystems configured to do so. Not all systems are expected to be able to trigger rollcall, but all systems must respond to it. Lights up LEDs for a set interval on every subsystem that recieves it.

docs.title: Improvements
docs.text: There were multiple ways to improve the hardware design in this subsystem. The three main ponts will be discussed here, but there is always room for improvement and it is not constrained to only these three ideas.

docs.title: Button Placement
docs.text:
To start, all of the buttons were used in the schematic. This was not the plan, but worked becasue of the spare buttons installed in case of emergencies. What this meant was that there were no more spare buttons. I would have added a few more buttons on the side to still keep the option of rerouting buttons in case of damage, wiring, or other issues.

Additionally, the buttons were all pressed together in a small format that resembles a D-pad controll, but I would have spaced them out a bit more so that the buttons could be pressed comfortably instead of having to arch each finger to press one button and advoid the others. This also goes with the boot and enable buttons. Since they are on seperate sides of the PCB, it was difficult to boot. I would have wanted another ground layer to move the Boot button next to the enable button or vice versus. This would keep them together and would ease the placement of other buttons so I am not fearing accidentially pressing either button.

docs.title: OLED Screen Flexibility
docs.text:
The OLED Screen was placed on the side of the PCB. Ther are two parts of this that I would change: the placements and the accessability. The OLED was placed in a way that it was facing left of the board. THis was an oversight on my part and I should have placed it facing downwards. Having it face downwards would make it easier to read the OLED screen instead of cranning your neck to look on the side of the pcb.

The other, more preferred, option would be to use wires and have a seperate housing for the OLED screen. This could work because the component on the PCB is a 4-pin connector housing. This would make it easy to get 4 wires and have the OLED connected outside the controller. By doing so, I could have used a bigger OLED and instead of each piece of information overwriting the other, I could have them seperated in their own sections.

docs.title: Size and Dimensions
docs.text: Lastly, the size of the PCB was bulky. I used up as much space as was allowed, but I think that did more harm than good. For the controller shousing it made it bulky and hard to handle. The sharp edges also cut into the hand if not using the housing. Overall, if the PCB could have been shaped more like a controller and less boxy, then there would be a better ease of use when using the PCB.

docs.title: Review of Module's Sucess
docs.text: The mudule hit most hardware requirements when created. The schematic was hastily done before it was origionally sent, but during PCB creation it was fixed up and worked as intended afterwards. The one part that the module failed was the up and down 8-pin connectors. The PCB footnote was to small and the Rx and Tx placements were not class standardized. This was an oversight on my part and I should have seen and fixed it, but seeing that there were only two people in the wireless controller and we had matching Rx and Tx we decided that it was okay and we went forward with the difference because at that point, we already had our PCBs.

docs.title: Startup Tip
docs.text:
1. I think that the most important thing to do is research and read datasheets for sensors. The main project I had problems with was the hall effect sensor. Half of the problem could have been avoided if I had started with reading the datasheet.
  2. I also think I should have read requirements more thouroughly and after each assignment. Even if you read the requirements, you will forget a few as you continue your project. Going back to them periodically could have helped save tiome and stress when finding parts of my project that were not up to standard.

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
1. Take your time to breathe when statring an assignment. If you rush this work, the next set of work will be rushed as well.
  2. Go back through your Github after every assignment to keep it up to date. This made the final report a cakewalk especially when you have finals around the corner.
  3. Read ahead for projects. If you don't you'll slowly get behind
  4. Communicate with your teammates. Each person has their specialty, if you are struggling, they may not be.
  5. Do not use AI to make your code. I saw a whole bunch of people do this last semester and when it came time to change the code they were clueless on how their code even worked. Use it to help you not do everything for you.
  6. Take time to know your classmates. They are there to help you and you should be there to help them.
  7. Time management is key when you want to get everything done. For most people, this is not their only class, but this will be a class that takes up most of your time. You should prepare for that while you are not in class. This is an easy class to fall behind in.
  8. The datasheets are there to guide you along your struggles. Most problems that I had could be solved when reading the data sheet and seeing that my pins were mistyped.
  9. Choose a project that you'll have fun with. The coding feels a lok easier and quicker when you enjoy what you are working on.
  10. Make lists and draw out assignments when working with teammates. Everyone has their own ideas in their head. If we don't show them to others, then we run the risk of miscommunication. It could be a small issue, or it could be a huge issue that will take everyone a lot of time to fix.

docs.title: Recommendations for Future Students
docs.text:
1. Learn to manage your time for this class and all your classes combined. It sounds like they are the same thing, they are not.
  2. Be thorough when creating your curcuits. One wrong move can make or break your board and it is easier to change that electronically than when you already have your PCB.
  3. Have fun when creating your projects. This is the time you are puting your designs in your mind into reality.
  4. Ask questions whenever you feel confused. If you don't speak up, you'll stay confused or use precious time to research it for hours. If your are learning it, ask then, it will save you time.
  5. Go to office hours. There are many people ther to help and your issue might have been the last issue someone else just solved.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This power budget was created to make sure that the wall power supply could supply the esp32. This is for a greander scheme of a whole system even though this subsystem does not use a whole lot of current.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text: From the prepare Power Budget, this subsystem has plenty of power from a 9V power supply. The only two main components are the esp32 and the OLED screen which means they come out to a little more than 500mA. This also means that the excess power can go to the next subsystem nearby which is the wir3eless system. The two subsystemsa are the only subsystems with this power since they are the remote control.
